nodes.referent: Morphophonology (also morphophonemics or morphonology), the branch of linguistics that studies the interaction between morphological structure (word formation, inflection, derivation) and phonological patterning -- specifically, how a morpheme's phonological shape alternates depending on its morphological environment (allomorphy, external/internal sandhi, ablaut/apophony, morphologically triggered vowel harmony or consonant mutation). It sits at the interface of subfield:morphology and subfield:phonology within field:linguistics; the term ('Morphonologie') was introduced by Nikolai Trubetzkoy in the late 1920s to name this as a distinct object of study. Distinct from morphology and phonology as standalone branches, and from generative phonology as one specific later theoretical framework for treating some of the same alternations.

nodes.rationale: Morphophonology is a well-established, commonly taught branch of linguistics distinct from both of its parent subfields (it is not simply 'phonology' or 'morphology' under another name -- it has its own object of study, the morphology-conditioned alternation), and the corpus already models comparable interface subfields elsewhere (e.g. subfield:computability-theory as an interface of subfield:mathematical-logic and subfield:theoretical-computer-science). Admitting it also lets the two person candidates in this batch earn their place at the correct grain instead of at the too-broad field:linguistics or subfield:phonology grain.

nodes.referent: Prince Nikolai Sergeyevich Trubetzkoy (1890-1938), Russian-born linguist and philologist, professor at the University of Vienna from 1922 until his death, and a founding member of the Prague Linguistic Circle. Son of the philosopher Sergei Nikolaevich Trubetskoy (first elected rector of Moscow University, d. 1905) -- not to be confused with his father, or with other members of the same princely Trubetskoy/Trubetzkoy family who were prominent academics in the same era. Author of the posthumously published Grundzuge der Phonologie (Principles of Phonology, 1939), the foundational text of Prague School structural phonology, which includes a dedicated chapter on 'Morphonologie'; earlier, in a paper of around 1929 in the Prague Circle's own Travaux, he introduced 'morphonologie' (morphophonology) as a named object of study distinct from phonology proper. Also worked on comparative Caucasian and Slavic historical linguistics and, separately, wrote on Eurasianism as a cultural-political movement. Not to be confused with any other linguist sharing the surname Trubetzkoy/Trubetskoy.

nodes.referent: Jan Ignacy Niecislaw Baudouin de Courtenay (1845-1929), Polish linguist of French Huguenot descent, who held professorships at Kazan, Dorpat (Tartu), Kraków, and St Petersburg/Petrograd. Founder, together with his student Mikolaj Kruszewski, of the Kazan School of linguistics; credited with an early, psychologically-grounded formulation of the phoneme as a functional unit of sound, and with distinguishing purely phonetically conditioned sound alternations ('divergences') from morphologically/grammatically conditioned ones ('correlations') in his 1890s work -- a distinction widely treated in histories of linguistics as the direct forerunner of what Trubetzkoy later named and systematized as morphophonology. Also worked on Slavic dialectology and general linguistic theory, and is credited with influencing Ferdinand de Saussure's structuralism. Not to be confused with any other bearer of the (uncommon) surname Baudouin de Courtenay.
